card.name: Limbo (dance)
card.tagline: A Trinidadian dance of endurance where performers arch backwards beneath a lowering bar.
card.profile: Limbo is a traditional dance and contest originating in Trinidad and Tobago, characterized by the performer arching their back to pass beneath a horizontal bar without touching it. Historically linked to funeral wakes and the cycle of life, it gained international fame in the 1950s through the performances of Julia Edwards. Today, it is widely recognized as a popular social game and tourist activity, though it retains deep roots in Afro-Caribbean cultural traditions.
card.insight: Emerging from 19th-century Tobagonian funeral wakes, the limbo symbolizes the cycle of life and death, with the dancer's emergence from beneath the bar representing a triumph over the grave.
card.profile_long:
The limbo is a dance and contest that originated in the mid-to-late 1800s on the island of Tobago. Historically, the dance was performed at funeral wakes, serving as a symbolic representation of the cycle of life and death. Participants would move under a pole that was gradually lowered from chest level, emerging on the other side as their heads cleared the pole, signifying the triumph of life over death. While some theories suggest the dance may be linked to the experience of enslaved people in the cramped galleys of slave ships, no literary reference has been found to substantiate this claim. The word 'limbo' itself is conjectured to be a derivative of the word 'limbus' or the English word 'limber'.

In the 1940s and 1950s, the dance underwent a significant transformation, moving from a traditional wake ritual to a form of popular entertainment. Edric Connor is credited with reviving the game in 1944, and the choreographer Julia Edwards, known as the 'First Lady of Limbo,' popularized the dance globally. Edwards introduced standard features such as the use of human bars formed by the limbs of other players and the incorporation of fire into the performance. Her company toured extensively throughout the Caribbean, Europe, North America, South America, Africa, and Asia during the 1960s. The dance's evolution and Edwards' contributions were later documented in the 2010 film 'Julia and Joyce' by Sonja Dumas.

Technically, the limbo is a contest of flexibility and balance. A horizontal bar is supported by two vertical poles. Contestants must pass under the bar with their backs facing the floor, bending backwards without touching the bar or the ground with any part of their body other than their feet. The bar is lowered after each successful round, and the contest continues until only one person remains. Professional limbo dancers often perform to specific Afro-Caribbean drum patterns. As the dance gained international popularity, it was integrated into pop music, most notably with Chubby Checker’s 1962 hit 'Limbo Rock' and the Soca song 'Limbo Break' by the Trinidadian Calypsonian Brigo.

Today, the limbo is considered the unofficial national game of Trinidad and Tobago. While it has largely disappeared from its original funeral context, it remains a staple of the Carnival season and is frequently used as a social 'icebreaker' in the tourism industry across the Caribbean. Despite its modern status as a party game, the physical demands of the dance are significant, leading to the development of specific injuries, sometimes referred to as 'limbostite,' which involve strains or tears in the groin area. World records for the lowest limbo clearance are held by individuals such as Dennis Walston and Shemika Charles, who have successfully navigated bars as low as 6 to 8.5 inches from the ground.

card.sacred_note: Historically associated with funeral wakes and the cycle of life and death; outsiders should respect its origins as a ritualistic practice rather than purely entertainment.

sections.origins_and_history: Originating in 19th-century Tobago, the limbo was traditionally performed at wakes. It is believed to be related to African legba or legua games and reflects the cycle of life. It was popularized in the 1950s by Julia Edwards.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Contestants pass under a horizontal bar with their backs facing the floor. Players must bend backwards without touching the bar or the floor with their hands. The bar is lowered after each round until only one player remains.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performances typically respond to Afro-Caribbean drum patterns. Popular music associated with the dance includes 'Limbo Rock' by Chubby Checker and 'Limbo Break' by Brigo.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance requires a horizontal bar supported by two vertical poles. Performances may include the use of fire.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically used at funeral wakes to symbolize the triumph of life over death. In modern contexts, it is used as a social icebreaker at resorts and during Carnival.
sections.notable_figures: Julia Edwards (First Lady of Limbo), Edric Connor, Dennis Walston, Shemika Charles, Brigo (Samuel Abrahams).
sections.lineage: Rooted in Afro-Caribbean cultural traditions and potentially linked to African legba or legua games.

claims.text: The limbo dates back to the mid to late 1800s in Tobago.
The dance originated as an event that took place at wakes in Tobago.
The game reflects the whole cycle of life, with the dancer emerging as a triumph of life over death.
Julia Edwards, known as the First Lady of Limbo, popularized the dance in the 1950s.
The dance is associated with injuries known as limbostite.
The world record for lowest limbo is held by Shemika Charles.
